notes:
I've written up notes on Leviticus 3 below. They're mostly the traditional reading. I could only search a limited number of times, so a lot is missing:

- **No sources found:** NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, Orthodox sources (oca.org), Lutheran, Methodist or Pentecostal teachers, and any prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching.
- **Labels:** The pages I read don't name their authors' denominations, so I report disagreements by teacher, not by tradition.
- **Guzik:** Enduring Word (David Guzik) is on your Pentecostal/charismatic list. His page gives no denomination, though.

## Overview (whole chapter)

- **Why it's called a peace offering:** Guzik says it was not given to *make* peace with God (the sin offering in ch. 4 did that) but to *enjoy* it. The peace offering was not an offering to *make* peace with God (this was the purpose of the sin offering of Leviticus 4), but an offering to *enjoy* peace with God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-3/
- **When it was given:** Ligonier lists three occasions: for thanksgiving, upon the payment of a vow, or as a free expression of the worshiper's goodwill (7:11–18). It was also the only sacrifice worshipers could eat. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/peace-offering
- **A shared meal:** Matthew Henry says God and his people ate together as friends. The meal could only happen if they were at peace, so it was a sign of fellowship and confirmed the covenant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/3.htm
- **Three shares:** Constable notes that God got the whole burnt offering and shared the grain offering with the priest. In the peace offering, God, priest and worshiper each got a part. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-3.html
- **The name:** An older note on Bible Hub's 3:1 page says "peace offering" means an offering made by people already at peace, not one that brings peace about. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/3-1.htm

## Verse by verse

**v. 1**
- **Male or female:** Guzik notes that, unlike the burnt offering, either sex was allowed. He links this to Galatians 3:28: all are welcome to fellowship with God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-3/
- Henry makes the same point: God looks at the heart, not the sex. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_003.cfm
- Bible Hub's study note says the stress is on taking part and giving thanks, not a narrow symbolic point. https://biblehub.com/leviticus/3-1.htm
- **Two symbolic readings:** One older commentary on Bible Hub says male and female picture Christ's strength in obeying and weakness in suffering. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/3-1.htm Kingcomments says the male stands for active obedience and the female for patient, submissive obedience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/king-en/leviticus/3.htm
- **Without blemish:** Guzik gives three meanings: give God your best; we need a sinless substitute; it points to Jesus (1 Peter 1:19). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-3/
- **Cattle first:** Ellicott explains the ox is listed first because it was the costliest animal. https://biblehub.com/leviticus/3-1.htm

**v. 2**
- **Laying on the hand (the readings differ):**
  - Guzik: as with the burnt offering, the worshiper identified with the substitute and symbolically passed his sin to it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-3/
  - The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary agrees: the offerer admitted he was guilty and deserved to die. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/leviticus-3.html
  - Henry: the offerer handed the animal over to God and named the mercies he was thanking God for, or made his request if it was a vow. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_003.cfm
  - Kingcomments: it is identification with the animal's *worth*, so God sees the worshiper "in the value of the offering." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/king-en/leviticus/3.htm
- **Who killed it:** Guzik thinks the worshiper *probably* made the cut himself (he's not certain). The priests then handled the blood, at the tabernacle entrance, as far in as a layman could go. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-3/
- **The blood:** Bible Hub's chapter notes say blood is shed even here, so peace with God is always "blood-bought" (Hebrews 9:22). https://biblehub.com/leviticus/3.htm

**vv. 3–4**
- **Which parts:** The Pulpit Commentary lists the inner fat, the kidneys and the lobe above the liver. Apart from the fat, the kidneys were the only thing burned. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/leviticus/3.htm
- **Why the fat:** Ellicott says "fat" means the best part, so it belonged to God and was not to be eaten. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-3.html
- **Symbolic readings:**
  - Guzik: fat is the animal's stored energy, a picture of giving God our energy and work. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-3/
  - Preacher's Homiletical: the inner fat showed inner health and pictures Christ's inmost excellence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/leviticus-3.html
  - Constable: since the Old Testament treats the kidneys and inner parts as the seat of feeling, they may stand for the worshiper's deepest emotions. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-3.html
- **The liver lobe:** Guzik quotes Peter-Contesse. Neighbouring peoples used the liver to tell fortunes, which may be why it had to be burned. It was also a delicacy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-3/

**v. 5**
- **"Atop the burnt offering":**
  - Henry: this was the daily morning lamb, so the peace offering added to it. Our thanks are accepted only once we are reconciled. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/3.htm
  - Coffman quotes Dummelow: part of the daily sacrifice was always smouldering, and The fire never went out. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/leviticus-3.html
  - Preacher's Homiletical: thanks and dedication follow Christ's atoning work and can't be offered apart from it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/leviticus-3.html
  - Guzik: the cross is both where sin is paid for and where we enjoy fellowship with God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-3/
- **"Pleasing aroma":** Guzik cites G. Campbell Morgan. The phrase is used for the first three offerings but not the sin or guilt offerings: fire brings out beauty in what is yielded and destroys what is condemned. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-3/
- **What happened to the meat:** The chapter doesn't say. Guzik explains it was shared by the priests and the worshiper's family. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-3/ Keil (quoted on Bible Hub) says tradition already set the meat aside for the meal, with details in 7:11–36. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/3-17.htm

**vv. 6–8**
- **Sheep or goats:** The same steps as for cattle apply, and the priests still handle the blood. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-3/
- **No birds:** Henry says birds were allowed for burnt offerings but not here. They have too little fat, and there would be almost nothing to share. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/3.htm Coffman adds that a bird couldn't feed the worshiper and his friends, so the poor lost nothing. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/leviticus-3.html
- **A lamb:** Kingcomments says it suggests gentleness, surrender and patiently bearing mistreatment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/king-en/leviticus/3.htm

**vv. 9–10**
- **The fat tail:**
  - Guzik says it was a delicacy that could weigh up to 60 lb (27 kg). It went to God, not to the meal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-3/
  - Peter-Contesse (quoted by Guzik) gives a lower figure, seven or more kilograms. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-3/
  - Bible Hub notes that carvings from ancient Ugarit show rams with oversized tails. https://biblehub.com/leviticus/3.htm
- **"Close to the backbone":** Kingcomments sees Christ's firmness against evil in the backbone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/king-en/leviticus/3.htm

**v. 11**
- **"Food":** Guzik calls it God's portion of a meal shared with the worshiper's family. He quotes Rooker that this meant fellowship with the Lord. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-3/
- Keil (on Bible Hub) explains "food of the firing" as food that reached the LORD by being burned. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/3-17.htm
- Preacher's Homiletical: God takes satisfaction in Christ's atoning sacrifice. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/leviticus-3.html

**vv. 12–15**
- **A goat:** The same steps as for the other animals. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-3/
- Kingcomments notes the goat was usually the sin-offering animal. It suggests worshipers whose thanks centre on sins forgiven, which is still a pleasing aroma. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/king-en/leviticus/3.htm

**v. 16**
- **"All the fat is the LORD's":** Guzik reads this as God's claim on all we value and on our energy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-3/
- Ellicott ties it closely to v. 17: because the fat is the Lord's, it must never be eaten. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-3.html

**v. 17**
- **Why God claimed fat and blood:**
  - Pulpit: These are forbidden to be eaten, as belonging to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/leviticus/3.htm
  - Poole and Benson give three reasons for the fat: reverence for the sacrifices, owning God as Lord of all creatures, and self-denial. For the blood: reverence, opposing idolaters who drank blood, and Christ's blood, which it pointed to. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/3-17.htm
  - Geneva Study Bible: eating fat symbolised carnality, eating blood cruelty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/3-17.htm
- **Which fat:** Henry says only the inner suet was banned, not fat mixed into the meat, even at home. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/3-17.html Jamieson-Fausset-Brown agrees the rest could be eaten. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/leviticus-3.html Clarke thinks the ban may have covered only the fat of sacrificial animals. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/3-17.html
- **"Permanent statute":** Ellicott prefers the wording "a statute for ever." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-3.html Guzik notes the phrase appears 17 times in Leviticus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-3/
- **Health reasons (offered as secondary):** Guzik says tapeworms often lived in fatty tissue. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-3/ A Bible Hub Q&A goes further and cites modern medical claims, while saying the main reasons are theological. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_ban_fat_and_blood_in_Leviticus_3_17.htm

## Where teachers differ

**Does v. 17 apply to Christians?**
- Gill says "perpetual" ran until the end of the Mosaic system, when the Messiah's blood was shed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/3-17.htm
- Coffman disagrees. He says the Jerusalem apostles made the blood ban a Christian rule too, and he notes some commentators argue it doesn't apply today. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/3-17.html
- Bible Hub's study note reads "wherever you live" as a lesson that obedience to God goes wherever we go. https://biblehub.com/leviticus/3-17.htm

**Is the peace offering a picture of the Lord's Supper?** (vv. 1–11)
- Rooker (via Precept Austin): the Israelite was God's guest at the meal, and believers likewise feast on the Lamb's body and blood at the Lord's Supper. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_3_commentary
- An older note on Bible Hub's 3:1 page says the peace offering foreshadows the Lord's Supper in the new dispensation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/3-1.htm
- Coffman links it to John 6: the victim's flesh fed the worshiper, as Christ's flesh and blood feed the believer. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/leviticus-3.html
- Kingcomments says that, like the peace offering, the Lord's Supper is not an obligation, though no one should skip it lightly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/king-en/leviticus/3.htm
- Kelly calls the peace offering "eucharistic," for shared joy and not for atonement. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/3-17.html

**Catholic reading**
- Catholic Answers treats Leviticus 3 as a picture of the Mass. It says that at the Last Supper Christ made the bread and wine into himself by his word so that he, as victim, could be shared as the peace offering of the New Testament. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/christs-peace-offering
- The Catholic New American Bible translates the term "communion sacrifice." https://biblehub.com/leviticus/3-1.htm

**Modern translations**
- The NRSV calls it a sacrifice of well-being. https://biblehub.com/leviticus/3-1.htm
- A bible.org writer says the name stresses complete well-being and harmony, not merely the absence of war. https://blogs.bible.org/the-five-fire-sacrifices-and-offerings-of-israel-the-peace-offering/
